FOREWORD

Indian Standard ( Part 4/Set 3 ) was adopted by the Indian Standards Institution on 31 January, 1984, after the draft finalized by the Packaging Code Sectional Committee had been approved by the Marine, Cargo Movement and Packaging Division Council. 0.2 The Packaging Code is being issued in the following one or more sections: Part Part Part Part Part Part Part Part 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 Product Packaging Ancillary Packages Packaging Storage Packaging Testing operations and transportation machinery packaging materials materials parts, each having

0.2.1 This section of the packaging code (Part 4/Set 3 ) deals with The properties and characteristics of plastics materials plastics packages. are described in Section 3 of Part 2, of the Packaging Code.

0.3 Development

of plastics containers is making rapid strides in the These containers are replacing the conventional packaging industry. containers such as metal and glass by virtue of their inherent advantages of light weight, strength and inert quality. Plastics containers are already in wide use in the food and drink, chemical, dairy, pharmaceutical, cosmetic and other industries. A plastics container may be accepted for packing a particular item or material provided its properties are compatiIt is technically possible to find a plastics ble with those of its contents. material suitable for the manufacture of a container for almost any given product, although this may not always be economically practicable. 2

IS : 10106 ( Part 4/Set 3 ) - 1984 0.4 In this section of the code, plastic containers
described This code the choice of Indian being currently used are and both their types and methods of manufacture are given. is, therefore, intended to assist the users of plastics containers in A complete list of the container most suitable for his purpose. Standards relating to plastic packaging is given in Appendix A.

0.5 In the preparation

of this standard considerable assistance has been code : Packaging derived from BS 1133 : Section 22 : 1967 ` Packaging in plastic containers `, issued by the British Standards Institution ( BSI ).

1. SCOPE 1.1 This section ( Part 4/Set 3 ) of the code lays down general on the use of packaging containers made of plastics materials.

METHODS

OF MANUFACTURE

used in the manufacture of a container depends to some extent on the nature of the plastics and the type of container to be made. The various processes used are as follows. 4.1 Blow

4.1.5 Stretch Blow Moulding - In this process an extruded or injection moulding preform is stretched in both directions for biaxial orientation in a blow moulded container to impart much improved physical and mechanical properties. The materials commonly used are PVC and PET. 4.1.6 Co-extruded Blow Moulding - In this process more than one polymer, such as SAN and PET, are used to form a parison for blow moulding. 4.2 Injection Moulding - This process is used for the production of thin-walled or thick-walled containers with open necks. In the injection moulding process, heat softened thermoplastics is forced into a mould by pressure and allowed to cool. The process may use single cavities or a mould containing many cavities. This process is also used for manufacture of transport container such as bottle crates, 4.3 Thermo-forming - In this process, heat softened sheet material is made to conform to a mould profile by using vacuum, pressure or mechanical aids. Different variations of forming in which combinations of vacuum, pressure and mechanical aids are used, have been developed in order to ensure more even material distribution. 4.4 Extrusion - This is used for the production of seamless thin-walled parallel sided containers. In the extrusion process a thermoplastic is softened by heat and pressure. The melt thus obtained is extruded through a sizing die after which it travels through a cooling zone, so as to retain its dimensional cross section. 4.5 Rotational Moulding - This process is a form of powder sintering in which plastics powder is introduced into a heated hollow metal mould which is then rotated in horizontal and vertical planes either in separate stages or simultaneously. The powder melts and takes the shape of the mould interior and is cooled before extraction as a complete moulding. moulding of plastics is 4.6 Compression Moulding - Compression employed mainly with thermosetting materials. A quantity of the material in powder, pallet, or dough form is placed in the lower cavity of a heated mould and compressed by lowering the upper half. The material is thus subjected to heat and pressure which causes it to flow and fill the contours of the mould. Thermosetting materials harden quickly under these conditions and can be ejcctcd without chilling the mould. 4.6.1 Transfer moulding is a modification of compression moulding whereby the material is first softened by heat in a chamber prior to being forced into a closed hcatcd mould for final curing. -~ ._ -*Specification for blown polyolefin plastic containers ( up to 5 litres ). 4

IS : 10106 ( Part 4/Set 3 ) - 1984 of thermoplastics can be carried out by 4.7 Fabrication - Fabrication welding or sealing, both of which rely on fusing or fluxing the mating surface generally under a certain amount of pressure. The heat shall be controlled to avoid marking, weakening or degrading the material and a number of methods have been developed to give the best results with The following welding processes are applidifferent plastics and shapes. cable. 4.7.1 Friction Welding - A pressure welding process in which faces to be united are softened by heat generated by friction. 4.7.2 Heated Tool Welding - A pressure welding process surfaces to be united are softened by conduction or radiation heated to 01s. 4.7.3 High Frequency Welding ( Dielectric Welding ) process in which the surfaces to be united are softened by a high frequency field. the sur-

in which the of heat from

A pressure welding by heat produced

4.7.4 HOS Gas Welding - A pressure welding process in which the surfaces to bc united are softened by a jet of hot air or inert gas produced by a welding torch. 4.7.5 Hot Wire Weldin,c - A welding process which utilizes a heated wire to weld and at the same time sever, films of plastics material; mainly confined to polyolefins. 4.7.6 Impulse Welding - A pressure welding process in which the surfaces to be united arc subjected to rapid heating followed by cooling, pressure being maintained over the whole of the cycle. 4.7.7 Induction Welding - A welding process in which the surfaces to be united are softened or melted by heat transfer from an electrical conductor The conductor is heated by the current embeded in the thermoplastics. induced by an alternating magnetic field. 4.7.8 Molten Bead Welding - A welding process in which the thermoplastic material at the joint is melted by the transfer of heat from an extruded bead on to the overlapping sheets. 4.7.9 Flame Welding - An edge welding process using a finely tipped flame for the heating of thermoplastic material, followed by cooling under pressure exerted by rollers. `I'his process is applied to thermoplastic films with a definite melting point such as polyolefins. 4.7.10 Ultmsonic Welding - A friction welding process in friction is illtcr-molrcl.rlar and is set up by ultrasonic vibration. 5 which the

IS : 10106 ( Part 4/&w 3 ) - 1984 4.7.11 Pressure Welding - Any welding process in which the weld is made by sustained pressure while the surfaces to be united are in a softened condition. 4.7.12 Seam Welding -- A pressure welding process which forms a continuous welded seam in which the surfaces to be united are softened either by heat produced by a high frequency field or by a conduction of heat from heated rollers or bars. The pressure may be applied continuously by rollers or progressively as in stitch welding. 5. METHODS OF TEST

6.8 Transport Containers - These unsupported drums, in a range of capacities from approximately 9-200 litres, are suitable for the transportation and storage of wide range of liquids (and solids) which require special precautions to guard against acidic or rust corrosion. They are usually made by either a blow moulding or a sintering process ( see Fig. 7A, 7B & 7C and IS : 6312-198Ot).
